essays.stem: You are the new sales manager for a distributor that supplies household goods to shops across Jamaica. Prepare an outline sales plan for the next year.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start from the company's goals and last year's results by product, customer and parish, and look at market trends, competitors and orders already in hand. From this I would set a yearly sales target, for example J$120,000,000, a 10% rise, with a gross margin target, and split it by quarter to allow for seasons such as back-to-school and Christmas. I would divide the island into territories and give each representative a target based on the area's potential and their experience, agreed with them. The plan would name priority products and customers, such as growing sales to supermarkets in the west, and the activities to reach them: regular visits, promotions with retailers and a trade fair. I would set out the resources needed: staff, vehicles, samples, stock levels agreed with the warehouse, and a sales budget. Service standards, such as delivery within 48 hours, would be agreed with operations. Finally I would set measures, including sales against target, margin, new accounts and on-time delivery, with monthly reviews.
markingPoints: Bases the plan on company goals, past results and the market
Sets a clear target and breaks it down by period and territory, agreed with staff
Names priority products, customers and sales activities
Plans resources, stock and service standards with operations
Sets measures and a regular review

essays.stem: Explain how you would monitor sales and service performance across a chain of five stores, and what you would do when a store falls short.
essays.modelAnswer: I would agree a small set of measures for every store: sales against target, gross margin, conversion rate, average transaction value, stock availability, customer satisfaction scores and complaints. Daily figures would come from the point-of-sale system into a dashboard, so I could compare stores and spot problems early. I would add a monthly mystery shopper visit and a short customer survey to check service, since figures alone do not show how customers are treated. Each week I would review results with the store managers, and each month I would visit each store. When a store falls short, I would first find the cause by breaking the figures down by product, day and staff member and by talking to the manager and staff. Causes might be low stock, poor staffing at busy times, weak product knowledge or a new competitor. I would then agree an action plan with the store manager, with clear steps, support, such as training or extra stock, and dates, and check progress weekly until results recover.
markingPoints: Sets balanced measures covering sales, margin and service
Uses system data and a dashboard to monitor regularly
Adds service checks such as mystery shopping and surveys
Finds the cause of a shortfall before acting
Agrees an action plan with support and follows it up

essays.stem: A company's sales staff are rewarded only on the value of sales they make, and complaints about service have risen. Evaluate the problem and recommend changes to the reward system.
essays.modelAnswer: A reward based only on sales value tells staff that selling is all that matters. Some may push products customers do not need, promise delivery dates the business cannot meet, give too many discounts or ignore after-sales problems that earn them nothing. This raises complaints and returns, harms the brand and can cost repeat business, so the company may gain sales now but lose profit and customers later. Staff who give good service may feel unfairly treated. I would recommend a balanced reward. Part of the bonus would still be based on sales against target, but part would be based on gross margin, customer satisfaction scores, complaint levels and repeat business. Sales lost through returns or cancelled orders would be taken off. Team rewards could be added so staff help each other. The new scheme should be explained clearly, tested for a quarter and reviewed. Training on needs-based selling and clear policies on discounts and delivery promises would support it.
markingPoints: Explains how a sales-only reward can harm service and customers
Notes the longer-term costs to profit, reputation and staff morale
Recommends a balanced reward including margin and service measures
Suggests safeguards such as deducting returns and team rewards
Plans to explain, trial and review the new scheme, with training

essays.stem: Describe how you would set, communicate and monitor service standards for a customer service team in a utility company.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start with what customers expect, using complaints, surveys and call records, and with the company's own aims. With the team, I would set clear, measurable standards, for example answering 80% of calls within 30 seconds, fixing 75% of queries on the first call, replying to e-mails within one working day and greeting every customer by name. Involving staff makes the standards realistic and builds commitment. I would write the standards on a single page, explain them at a team meeting and in induction, and show staff how to meet them through training and role play. Standards would be displayed and reviewed in the weekly team meeting. To monitor them, I would use the call system's reports, listen to a sample of calls with a checklist, read customer survey results and track complaints. Results would be shared with the team each week and with each person in one-to-ones, with praise for good work and coaching where needed. I would review the standards every six months as customer needs and systems change.
markingPoints: Bases standards on customer expectations and company aims
Sets clear, measurable standards with the team
Communicates the standards through briefings, induction and training
Monitors with system data, call checks, surveys and complaints
Shares results, coaches staff and reviews the standards

essays.stem: Explain how a manager can make sure that what the sales team sells is delivered on time and as promised.
essays.modelAnswer: The first step is to make the sales and delivery teams work as one system. The manager would map the process from order to delivery: taking the order, checking stock and credit, picking, packing, invoicing and delivery. Sales staff need accurate, live information on stock levels and realistic delivery times, so they only promise what can be done. Orders should be entered once, correctly, into a shared system, with a check of the details with the customer. The sales forecast should be shared with purchasing and the warehouse so that stock and vehicles are ready for busy periods. A service standard, such as delivery within 48 hours, should be agreed and measured as an on-time-in-full rate. The manager would hold a short weekly meeting between sales and operations to review late or wrong orders and fix their causes. Customers should be told quickly if a delay occurs. Finally, complaints and returns would be tracked by cause, so repeated problems are found and removed.
markingPoints: Maps the process from order to delivery
Gives sales staff accurate stock and delivery information so promises are realistic
Shares forecasts so stock and transport are ready
Sets and measures a delivery standard such as on-time-in-full
Reviews failures with operations, informs customers and removes causes

essays.stem: Plan the staff and other resources a large retail store in Kingston needs for the back-to-school sales season.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start with last year's sales by week and by department for July to September, adjust them for this year's forecast and note the busiest days and hours. From this I would work out how many cashiers, floor staff and stock handlers are needed at each time. I would plan the roster early, limit leave during the peak, offer extra hours to part-time staff and hire and train temporary staff by early July. Every new person would get a short induction on the tills, the returns policy, service standards and safety. I would agree stock levels with purchasing for uniforms, shoes, bags, books and stationery, and arrange extra deliveries and storage. I would check that tills, card machines and the stock system are working and that there is a backup if the power or network fails. I would set up clear signs, extra queue lanes and a schedule for refilling shelves. During the season I would monitor sales, queues and stock each day and adjust the roster, and afterwards review what worked.
markingPoints: Uses past sales and the forecast to plan staffing by day and hour
Plans rosters, leave, temporary staff and their training early
Plans stock and deliveries with purchasing
Checks equipment and systems, with backups, and plans the store layout
Monitors daily during the season and reviews afterwards

essays.stem: Explain, in general terms, the legal and ethical duties a manager must keep in mind when managing sales and service.
essays.modelAnswer: Consumer protection law, in general, expects goods and services to match their description, be of fit quality and do what they are sold for, and expects sellers not to mislead customers about price, quality or terms. Prices should be clearly shown and charged correctly, and returns, refunds and warranties handled fairly and as the policy and the law require. Tax law means the business must record every sale and give proper receipts showing GCT at the current rate where it applies. The data protection law means customer information should be collected for a clear purpose, kept secure and not shared without good reason. Contracts with business customers, including credit terms and service level agreements, must be honoured. Ethically, staff should sell to customers' needs, not use pressure or false promises, and treat every customer with respect, whatever their background. A manager should make sure staff know the policies, should design rewards that do not encourage poor practice, and should check that complaints are handled properly.
markingPoints: Goods and services must match descriptions and be of fit quality
Prices, returns and refunds must be fair and as stated
Sales must be recorded and receipts show GCT where it applies
Customer data must be protected and contracts honoured
Ethical selling, respect for customers and policies that support them

essays.stem: Explain how you would collect customer feedback and use it to improve sales and service delivery.
essays.modelAnswer: I would collect feedback in several ways so that the picture is complete. A short survey by text message or tablet just after purchase would give quick scores. Complaints and compliments from every channel, including the counter, phone, e-mail and social media, would be logged in one place with their cause. Sales staff would note what customers ask for that we do not stock, and why sales are lost. A mystery shopper would check service against our standards each month, and I would talk to some key customers each quarter. Each month I would analyse the feedback, looking for patterns, such as many complaints about delivery in one parish or low scores at one branch. I would share the results with the team and ask for their ideas. The most important problems would be tackled first, with a named owner and a date, for example changing delivery routes or retraining staff. I would then check whether scores and complaints improved, and tell customers what changed because of what they said.
markingPoints: Uses several feedback methods, including surveys, complaints and mystery shopping
Logs feedback in one place with causes
Analyses patterns regularly
Involves the team and acts on the main problems with owners and dates
Checks whether things improved and reports back to customers

essays.stem: Describe how you would develop the skills of a sales and service team so that both sales and customer satisfaction improve.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first find the training needs by looking at each person's results, observing them with customers and asking them where they need help. A newer person might need product knowledge and needs-based selling, while an experienced one might need help with negotiation or handling difficult customers. I would plan a mix of methods. Product training and fact sheets would come from suppliers. Short sessions at weekly meetings would cover one skill at a time, such as asking open questions, handling objections or explaining warranties. Role plays would let staff practise before using a skill with customers. On the floor, I would coach each person after watching them, giving specific, balanced feedback. Strong performers could mentor new staff. Each person would have a simple development plan, reviewed every quarter. I would measure the results by watching conversion rates, average sale value, complaints and satisfaction scores, both for each person and for the team. Good progress would be recognised publicly, which helps keep staff motivated.
markingPoints: Identifies each person's training needs from results, observation and discussion
Uses a mix of methods, such as product training, short sessions and role play
Coaches on the job with specific feedback and uses mentoring
Sets individual development plans and reviews them
Measures the effect on sales and service and recognises progress

essays.stem: A hardware business sells only from its store in May Pen. Evaluate adding field sales representatives and online ordering, and recommend a way forward.
essays.modelAnswer: Selling only from the store keeps costs low and lets customers see and handle goods, but it limits sales to people who come in. Field sales representatives could visit contractors, builders and farms across Clarendon and Manchester, build relationships and win larger repeat orders. However, they add salary, vehicle and commission costs, and need targets, routes and close management to pay their way. Online ordering, with delivery or collection, would reach busy customers and those further away, and could run all day. It needs an accurate catalogue, prices kept up to date, secure payment, stock information that is correct and a reliable delivery service, or it will cause complaints. It also needs someone to manage it. I would recommend starting with online ordering for collection and local delivery, since it costs less, and testing one field representative focused on contractors for six months, with clear targets. Both would be judged on extra gross profit against their costs, and on customer feedback, before the business expands either.
markingPoints: Notes the strengths and limits of store-only selling
Evaluates field sales: benefits, costs and management needs
Evaluates online ordering: benefits and what must be in place
Makes a clear, staged recommendation
Sets measures such as extra profit against cost and customer feedback

practical1.title: Prepare a quarterly sales and service delivery plan for a branch
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a case about a made-up branch of a Jamaican retailer or distributor (for example an appliance store in Montego Bay), with last year's sales by month and product, staff numbers, current service problems and the company's growth target. As a group, prepare a sales and service delivery plan for the next quarter. Give each member a named role: sales planner (sets the quarter's target and splits it by month and by salesperson, with reasons), staffing planner (writes a roster for one busy week that matches staff to the busiest times), service standards lead (writes a one-page service standards card with at least five measurable standards), dashboard builder (builds a simple spreadsheet dashboard with the measures and targets, checking every figure twice), and presenter (presents the plan to the assessor in 10 minutes as if to the area manager). In a group of four, the sales planner also presents.
materials: Case brief and sales data from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and word processor software
photos: The target split by month and by salesperson
The roster for a busy week
The dashboard spreadsheet on screen with measures and targets
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the plan
Target is based on the data and growth goal, and the split adds up correctly
Roster matches staffing to the busiest times
Service standards are clear and measurable
Dashboard shows sensible measures with correct targets
Presented clearly and answered the assessor's questions
safety: Use made-up names for staff and customers
Treat the case data as confidential; return printouts to the assessor
Plan rosters that respect rest breaks and fair hours
Share the workload fairly and take a short screen break

practical2.title: Analyse sales and service results and run a sales team meeting to agree actions
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a spreadsheet of one month's results for a made-up sales team of six people: sales against target, conversion rate, average sale value, returns, complaints and on-time delivery. First, analyse the results. Then role-play a 20-minute sales team meeting to review them and agree actions, with other members playing team members. Give each member a named role: analyst (works out each person's and the team's results against target in the spreadsheet, checking every figure twice), chair (the sales manager, who leads the meeting, keeps it to time and makes sure everyone is heard), service lead (presents the complaints and delivery figures and their likely causes), note-taker (records the discussion and writes an action plan with owners and dates), and observer (watches the meeting with a checklist and gives feedback on how it was run). In a group of four, the chair also gives the observer's feedback at the end. Feedback in the meeting must be about results and behaviour, not about people's character.
materials: Team results spreadsheet from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and word processor software
Meeting room with a table and chairs
photos: The spreadsheet on screen with results against target
The chart of team results shown in the meeting
The action plan with owners and dates
checklist: Took a named role and carried it out
Results against target are correct and were checked twice
Causes of gaps are discussed using the data, not blame
Meeting keeps to time and every member is heard
Action plan has clear actions, owners and dates
safety: Use made-up names; do not discuss real colleagues' performance
Treat the results data as confidential staff information
Keep the role play respectful; disagree with ideas, not people
Stop the role play if anyone becomes uncomfortable, and tell the assessor
